questions.knowledge_point: Comparing Slopes of Functions at Different Points
questions.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14039985/assets/5e232394bb3f520386068110e42887faa288c31077a660570494ccc5a85b0486.png)

Given the graph of $y=f(x)$ above, which of the following statements is true?
questions.worked_solution:
From the graph, we see that

- The slope of the tangent at $x=-1$ is zero, so ${f}^{′}(-1)=0.$

- The slope of the tangent at $x=0$ is negative, so ${f}^{′}(0)<0.$

- The slope of the tangent at $x=1$ is positive, so ${f}^{′}(1)>0.$

Therefore, ${f}^{′}(0)<{f}^{′}(-1)<{f}^{′}(1).$

Consider the graph of $y=f(x)$ above. Which of the following statements is true?
questions.worked_solution:
From the graph, we see that

- The slope of the tangent at $x=-4$ is positive, so ${f}^{′}(-4)>0.$

- The slope of the tangent at $x=-3$ is zero, so ${f}^{′}(-3)=0.$

- The slope of the tangent at $x=-1$ is negative, so ${f}^{′}(-1)<0.$

Therefore, ${f}^{′}(-1)<{f}^{′}(-3)<{f}^{′}(-4).$

questions.knowledge_point: Determining the Intervals on Which a Function Is Decreasing Using Differentiation
questions.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14039985/assets/6c3a45ac200d1f65c326354297e6e03b5347b4d4ec3fbb2a99bb7cde98376db8.png)

Find the values of $x$ for which the function $g(x)=\frac{2\operatorname{ln}⁡(3x)}{x}$ (plotted above) is strictly decreasing.

$x\in (${{field-1}}$,$
{{field-2}}$)$
questions.worked_solution:
The function is strictly decreasing where ${g}^{′}(x)<0.$ Differentiating $g(x)$ using the quotient rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{g}^{′}(x) & =\frac{(\frac{2}{3x}\cdot 3)x-2\operatorname{ln}⁡(3x)}{{x}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{2-2\operatorname{ln}⁡(3x)}{{x}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{2(1-\operatorname{ln}⁡(3x))}{{x}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

So we need to solve the inequality

$$
\frac{2(1-\operatorname{ln}⁡(3x))}{{x}^{2}}<0.
$$

Since $x>0$ is the domain of $g$ and ${x}^{2}>0$ for $x>0,$ the denominator is positive; thus this reduces to

$$
1-\operatorname{ln}⁡(3x)<0.
$$

Solving $\operatorname{ln}⁡(3x)=1$ gives the critical point

$$
x=\frac{e}{3}.
$$

From the graph, this critical point is a maximum. The slope of the tangent lines is positive to the left of the critical point and negative to the right of the critical point. 

So, we summarize the sign of the derivative in the following table:

$$
\left.\begin{aligned}x & (0,\frac{e}{3}) & \frac{e}{3} & (\frac{e}{3},\infty ) \\ g & ↗ & \text{max} & ↘ \\ {g}^{′} & + & 0 & -\end{aligned}\right|
$$

Finally, we conclude that the function is strictly decreasing on the interval $(\frac{e}{3},\infty ).$

questions.knowledge_point: Determining the Intervals on Which a Function Is Increasing Using Differentiation
questions.problem:
Find the values of $x$ for which the function $g(x)=({x}^{2}-3){e}^{x}$ is strictly increasing.

$x<$
{{field-1}} $\,$ and $\,x>$
{{field-2}}
questions.worked_solution:
The function is strictly increasing where ${g}^{′}(x)>0.$ Differentiating $g(x)$ using the product rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{g}^{′}(x) & =({x}^{2}-3){e}^{x}+2x\,{e}^{x} \\  & =({x}^{2}+2x-3){e}^{x},\end{aligned}
$$

so we need to solve the inequality

$$
({x}^{2}+2x-3){e}^{x}>0.
$$

Since ${e}^{x}>0$ for all real $x,$ this reduces to

$$
{x}^{2}+2x-3>0.
$$

The above inequality factors as

$$
(x+3)(x-1)>0.
$$

The graph of $y=(x+3)(x-1)$ has roots at $x=-3$ and $x=1,$ as shown below:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14039985/assets/9b847390fb6de568144d309c45fb8c904475bdde79a46a90ec0fd4426a71b57b.png)

For an upward-opening parabola, the product $(x+3)(x-1)$ is positive when $x<-3$ or $x>1.$

Therefore, we conclude that the function is strictly increasing on the intervals 

$$
x<-3\,\text{and}\,x>1.
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Determining the Intervals on Which a Function Is Decreasing Using Differentiation
questions.problem:
Given that $f(x)=\frac{2}{5}\sqrt{{x}^{5}}-\frac{4}{3}\sqrt{{x}^{3}}+2$ is defined for $x\in (0,\infty ),$ find the values of $x$ for which the function is strictly decreasing.

$x\in (${{field-1}}$,$
{{field-2}}$)$
questions.worked_solution:
We first write $f(x)$ as

$$
f(x)=\frac{2}{5}{x}^{5/2}-\frac{4}{3}{x}^{3/2}+2.
$$

The function is strictly decreasing where ${f}^{′}(x)<0.$ Differentiating $f(x),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{2}{5}\cdot \frac{5}{2}{x}^{3/2}-\frac{4}{3}\cdot \frac{3}{2}{x}^{1/2} \\  & ={x}^{3/2}-2{x}^{1/2} \\  & ={x}^{1/2}(x-2) \\  & =(x-2)\sqrt{x},\end{aligned}
$$

so we need to solve the inequality

$$
(x-2)\sqrt{x}<0.
$$

The expression $\sqrt{x}$ is always positive. So, this reduces to

$$
x-2<0.
$$

Solving this inequality, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x-2 & <0 \\ x & <2.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since the function is restricted to $x\in (0,\infty ),$ we conclude that $f(x)$ is strictly decreasing on the interval $x\in (0,2).$
